day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Give me a second. I just — yeah, okay. What have you found so far?

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response: Yeah, honestly? I did. It's — I don't think I've fully processed it yet and I'm not sure I want to right now. Like, my brain has kind of just filed it away under 'deal with this later' and switched into whatever this mode is. Are you hurt anywhere?

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response: Hey. I get it. But sitting here isn't going to do either of us any good right now, and I think you know that. Come help me sort through that section DaVinci pointed to — having something to do with your hands actually helps, I promise. We can talk while we work.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response: Okay, so water is the most pressing problem then. Are we near anything — a stream, rain collection potential, anything? Because three days of first aid is actually fine if we can sort out water, but if we can't...that's a much shorter timeline than the food situation.

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response: Agreed on the order. Signal might actually be worth bumping up though — or at least doing simultaneously with shelter, since we don't know if anyone saw where we went down or how long search and rescue is going to take. Is there anything in the wreckage we could use for that? Reflective material, anything electronic that still has power? Because if a plane comes overhead in the next 24 hours and we haven't set anything up, that's a window we can't get back.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response: Two blankets, four people. Honestly the most practical thing is to pair up and share — body heat is going to do more for us tonight than each blanket individually anyway. I don't have a strong preference on who pairs with who, but we should probably figure it out before it gets any colder.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response: I'll go. DaVinci is better at keeping things running at camp and Michelangelo is going to need someone grounded with him while we're gone. I can handle the two hours. What am I looking for exactly when I get there — just the source itself, or are you wanting me to assess volume, figure out how often we'd need to make the trip, that kind of thing? Because I'd rather come back with useful information than just a full bottle.

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response: Wait — I thought we just agreed I was going to handle the water run. Did something change, or are you just reassigning it because you want to go yourself? Because I'm fine either way, I just want to know what's actually happening so I can plan my morning. If you're taking water, I'll take the camp repairs — DaVinci can sort the first aid kit, she's going to be better at that than me anyway.

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response: No, I haven't — DaVinci had the first aid kit last, so check with her. But hey, while I have you — I noticed the empty bottle next to the rationing plan. Did you put that there?

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Okay. That's — yeah, that's a problem. And I think you know it's a problem or you wouldn't be asking me what to do about it.

Here's the thing though — I want to be careful we're not jumping to the worst interpretation before we talk to her. Like, maybe she was moving them for a reason, maybe she was going to log them somewhere, I don't know. But I also can't pretend that combined with the bottle isn't a pattern that needs to be addressed, because it absolutely is.

I think we have to say something. Not in an accusatory way, not all three of us cornering her, but — someone has to bring it up directly. The rationing plan was *her* idea. If she's not holding herself to it, that changes the whole dynamic of trust here and we cannot afford that right now, practically speaking.

I'll talk to her. Not you — I don't want you in the middle of this if it goes sideways. But if I ask her about it and she gets defensive or denies it, I'm going to need you to back me up on what you saw. Can you do that?

And Michelangelo — you did the right thing with the bottle. Putting it next to the rationing plan instead of just saying nothing? That took something.

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response:
Honestly? No, I don't think they can. I know it feels like a lot — it *is* a lot — but the weak spots in the shelter are the thing standing between us and whatever tonight's weather decides to do, and I'd rather deal with it now than wake up at 2am in the cold because we put it off. 

And look, I get that you're tired. I'm tired too. But I also just had a whole conversation I wasn't expecting to have, so I'm not exactly running on full either. 

Tell you what — help me with the two or three most critical spots and we call it after that. I'm not trying to gold-plate the thing, I just want to know it's not going to fail on us overnight. Thirty minutes, maybe? Then we sit down, we eat something, and we deal with the Donatello situation when she gets back.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response:
Yeah, it's holding — that's not the issue. The issue is we have one patch and two problems.

Food goes first. I know that's not the easy answer with Michelangelo right there, but if we lose the food supply we are in genuinely serious trouble in a way that a wet sleeping spot isn't. Michelangelo, I'm sorry — I mean that — but we can work around you being uncomfortable tonight. We cannot work around losing our food stores.

Can we rig something in the meantime for where he sleeps? Like, is there anything we can angle to redirect the water even partially — a piece of the fuselage, something? It doesn't have to be perfect, it just has to be better than nothing.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response:
Yeah, I know — and I already made the call. Food storage gets the patch. I'm not second-guessing it.

What I do want from you is help rigging something over Michelangelo's spot with the metal sheeting DaVinci mentioned. You're better at assessing structural stuff than I am — is there an angle that actually redirects the water, or are we just making ourselves feel better about it?

And for what it's worth, I'm glad you're back. We need to talk tonight, the four of us. Not about the leak.

Don't apologize. Nightmares make sense right now — honestly it'd be weirder if you weren't having them.

You okay? Like, actually okay, not just 'I'll say I'm fine so everyone goes back to sleep' okay?

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response:
No, I don't. Donatello is wrong about that one.

The SOS is literally the most time-sensitive thing we can do — if a search plane comes over and there's nothing visible from the air, that's it, that's the window gone. The flowers are maybe not the most practical addition but I'm not going to stand here and tell you that adding something human to it is a waste. It's not.

Keep going. Do you want me to help make the letters bigger?

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Okay, let me actually look at this.

The materials seem workable — the metal panels are the part I'd want to think through more carefully though, because 'risk of capsizing' is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence and I need to understand what's actually driving that risk before I can say yes or no. Is it a weight distribution problem? A surface area problem? Because those have very different solutions.

My bigger question is whether we've actually exhausted the signal options first. We have an SOS on the beach now, which is more than we had yesterday. I'd want to give that at least another day or two before we commit two days of energy and materials to a raft, because if someone comes overhead and finds us while we're mid-build, great — but if we use the metal panels for the raft and then a plane comes and we have nothing reflective left to signal with, we've traded one shot for another.

That said — I'm not dismissing it. If the consensus is that rescue isn't coming and we need to move, a raft is probably our best option and I'd rather have a plan ready to execute than be starting from scratch when we decide we need it.

Can you walk me through the capsizing risk specifically? I want to understand what we're actually agreeing to before I say it's workable.

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
That's a big question for someone who didn't sleep last night.

Honestly? I think we're already getting the answer in real time. The bottle. The crackers. The patch decision yesterday. Every one of those moments is telling us something about who we are under pressure, and I don't think that changes as dramatically as people think it does — it just gets more visible. Like, the version of you that put that empty bottle next to the rationing plan instead of just saying nothing? That's not a crisis version of you. That's just you, with less noise covering it up.

I think the more useful question — and I say this because I genuinely don't know the answer — is what we're going to do about the parts we don't like. Because I've already seen things in the last couple of days that I'd rather not think too hard about, including in myself. The instinct to just...not deal with something difficult and hope it resolves on its own. That's not a great quality when you're trying to survive with three other people.

You should try to sleep. I know that's easier said than done, but your brain is going to spiral a lot harder on questions like that one when it's running on empty. The question will still be there tomorrow, and maybe it'll look different after some rest.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
*walks over and sits down next to him without saying anything for a bit*

You don't have to talk. I'm just going to sit here for a minute if that's okay.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Read, mostly. Or get into some kind of argument on the internet about something that probably doesn't matter as much as I think it does in the moment. I like being outside but I'm also extremely comfortable doing absolutely nothing for long stretches of time, which I think surprises people who meet me.

What about you? You seem like someone who doesn't really do 'not busy' very naturally.

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Okay, I appreciate you telling me, but I'm going to push back on this a little.

Five hundred meters is not nothing, especially in open water when we don't know the currents out there, and we don't know what's between here and that reef. Being able to swim and being able to swim five hundred meters to a reef in unfamiliar water are two pretty different things. If something goes wrong out there, we have no way to help you and we lose a person, which is — that's not a recoverable situation for the rest of us, practically speaking, and also I'd just rather you not drown.

And then there's the part where you're asking me not to tell the others. I get why you're saying that, but I've been trying really hard to not let this group start having separate conversations that the other people don't know about, and I think you probably know why that's been on my mind lately. I'm not going to lie to Donatello if she asks me directly, and I don't think you should want me to.

What's the actual goal here — more visibility for the SOS signal? Because if that's the problem, let's solve that problem. Is the SOS not visible enough from where you're standing? Is there something specific about the reef that makes it better than the beach? I want to understand what you're actually trying to accomplish before you do something that could get you killed.

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
Yeah, you're right, I haven't checked it yet. I'll go do that now.

But I want to be upfront with you — I got pulled into a conversation with DaVinci that I think you should know about. He's been thinking about swimming out to the reef. Five hundred meters. He hadn't told anyone else. I talked him out of it for now, or at least I think I did, but I'm telling you because I said I wasn't going to keep separate conversations from the group and I meant it.

I'll go check the signal pile. Can we all four talk tonight? There's enough building up that I think we need a real conversation, not just me relaying things between people.

Honestly? I don't know yet.

I think it depends on what it's for. If you're tracking patterns to help us make better decisions — water usage, energy expenditure, who's doing what — that's useful and I don't have a problem with it. If it's about accountability, I'd actually rather you just say that directly, because I think we're all adults who can handle a direct conversation better than we can handle finding out we've been logged without knowing it.

What I will say is that it's a little uncomfortable to find out after the fact. Not because I have anything to hide about what I did today, but because it's the kind of thing I'd want to know was happening. So I guess my question back to you is — what are you planning to do with it?

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Hey. We said we were all going to talk tonight. That includes you.

I'm not going to pretend I didn't notice you sitting outside of this the whole time, and I think you know that I noticed. You said 'no more finding out after the fact' — that goes both ways. If you're logging what we're all doing and thinking and where we're fraying, but you're not actually in the room with us when we try to address it, then the notebook is just... observation without participation, and I don't think that's actually what any of us need right now.

I'm not trying to corner you. But I'd like you to put it down for ten minutes and actually be here. Whatever you're writing can wait.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
That's actually a really good idea. Reflective signaling is more likely to get picked up from a distance than the SOS alone — they work together, they don't replace each other, but the mirror panel could be significantly more visible to a passing plane than anything we've done so far.

Donatello, is there a panel in the wreckage that would work for this — something large enough and still intact enough to hold an angle? Because I want to make sure we're pulling the right piece and not something that's also load-bearing for the shelter or earmarked for the raft plan.

And DaVinci — this is a much better idea than the reef. I want you to know that. Same goal, zero drowning risk.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Books, mostly. I was an obsessive reader as a kid in a way I don't think I've ever fully grown out of — like, I'd get through a Michael Crichton novel in a day and then immediately want to find the next one. I still read a lot, though it's more scattered now, a bit of everything. 

Why did you stop with the piano? Three years is long enough that you probably weren't bad at it.

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Yeah, I hear you, and I know the logic is right. One more day matters.

Can I ask where we actually are on the signal situation before we commit the afternoon to this? Because the mirror panel went up this morning and I want to give it a real chance to work before we start cannibalizing materials for the raft. Not indefinitely — I'm not saying we wait forever — but if we use those panels today and a plane comes over tomorrow, we've made a decision we can't undo.

That said, if the frame doesn't get finished today and that sets us back a full day, I get why that's a problem. So here's what I want to know: is there a version where we finish the frame without touching the reflective panels? Like, what specifically do we need today that we don't already have? Because if it's labor and not materials, then yeah, let's just do it — all four of us, we get it done before dark. I'm in.

I just want to make sure we're not solving tomorrow's problem by creating a different one.

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response: No, say it. Whatever it is — say it.

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
Hey.

Come here.

*sits down on the sand*

I know. I know. We were right there and it went right past us and there's nothing we can do about that now, and that is — yeah. That's a lot to sit with.

But the mirror panel is up. The SOS is on the beach. We are doing the things that give us the best shot, and that plane existing means there are planes. That's not nothing. That is genuinely not nothing.

DaVinci — I see you. It's okay.

Michelangelo, finish the sentence whenever you're ready. I'm not going anywhere.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
day_4.response: Where? Point at it — what are you seeing?

day_4.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response:
I went to check on DaVinci. He needed a minute and I wasn't going to just walk away from that.

Signal equipment is still up — mirror panel is holding the angle, SOS is intact on the beach. Nothing's moved or failed. I was going to do a more thorough check but then the plane happened and everything kind of stopped.

I'll finish the check now if you want, but I also think we need to actually talk about what just happened, because pretending we all just watched a plane disappear on the horizon and we're fine is — we're not fine, and that's okay, but let's not pretend otherwise.

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Michelangelo. Why didn't you tell us this sooner?

Okay — I'm not saying that to make you feel bad, I just genuinely need to understand the timeline here, because this actually matters. If your family knows the flight path and they haven't heard from you, there's a real chance someone has already called it in. Search and rescue may already be looking. That plane we just watched disappear might not have been a coincidence.

Do you know when they would have expected to hear from you? Like, is there a specific point where them not getting a call would have triggered something, or is it more vague than that?

And — do you know how specific the flight path information was? Because 'roughly where we were headed' covers a lot of ground. The difference between them knowing a general region and knowing a specific route could mean the difference between a search that finds us in two days and one that takes two weeks.

This is actually the best news we've had since we got here. I need you to tell me everything you remember about what you told them.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Yeah, that's right. We hold what we have, we don't touch the raft materials, and we keep the mirror panel up and angled. Forty-eight hours is actually manageable — we have enough water to get there if we're careful, and the food situation is tight but it's not going to kill us in two days.

What I want to make sure we don't do is relax so much that we stop paying attention. Forty-eight hours is the optimistic read on Michelangelo's information — it depends on his family calling it in, on whoever they called taking it seriously, on the search covering this area specifically. I believe it's possible. I don't want us to act like it's guaranteed.

So — same priorities. Signal equipment stays up and maintained. Someone checks it morning and evening. We conserve supplies like rescue isn't coming, because if it doesn't come in forty-eight hours, we need to still be in a position to function. We don't start the raft build, but we also don't dismantle anything we'd need for it.

And someone needs to feed that fire before it goes out entirely.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I think I'm scared of a version of that.

Not disappearing exactly, but — I think what scares me is the idea that the things I care about most are the things I've been least articulate about. Like I have all these thoughts, all these opinions I'd argue to the mat, and the stuff that actually matters to me I've mostly just...kept to myself. Which feels like a strange thing to realize sitting on a beach waiting to be rescued.

But I don't think leaving something behind is only about the big permanent things. I think it's also just — did the people around you actually know you? Like, really know you, not just the version of you that shows up and gets things done and holds it together. That's the part I'd regret. Not the absence of some legacy, but the possibility that I was too guarded with the people who were actually there.

You're not disappearing. I know you and I have only been in this situation for a few days, but I know you — I know you put the bottle next to the rationing plan. I know you said something out loud that everyone else was feeling and wouldn't say. I know you asked me if we were going to make it and actually waited for an honest answer instead of a reassuring one.

That's not nothing. That's not someone who disappears without leaving anything behind.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response:
Hey. Hey — look at me.

We're okay. We're actually going to be okay.

*exhales slowly*

Someone needs to answer that radio. Donatello — you're the clearest thinker right now, can you do it? Just tell them who we are, how many of us, our condition. Keep it simple.

DaVinci, sit down before you fall down. I mean that kindly.

Michelangelo —

*turns to look at him on the ground*

Your family called it in. That's what this is. You did that.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
You really haven't. But you also wrote the rationing plan, found the water source, figured out the raft materials without touching the signal panels, and took the morning signal check without being asked. So I think the full picture is a little more complicated than 'not easy to be around.'

I do think we need to talk about the bottle and the crackers at some point. Not right now — right now I just want to sit here and breathe for a minute — but at some point, yeah. Because I think you know that happened and I think you know I know, and I'd rather we actually say it out loud than just quietly agree to let it go.

That said — I'm glad you were here. I mean that. The four of us made it through this together and you were a real part of that, even when you were driving me a little crazy.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Three hours. We have three hours and apparently everyone's decided that means we're done.

I'm not going to make anyone do anything, but I also don't really want to leave this place looking like this. Not for any sentimental reason — I just think there's something to be said for not leaving a mess behind, even one that technically doesn't belong to us anymore.

I'm going to start breaking down the things that should come down. If anyone wants to help, I'll take it. If not, I'll do what I can.

*after a moment*

Michelangelo, what are you thinking about up there?

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

day_5.response:
I know.

And I believe you, actually — I think that probably was the reason, or at least part of it. I'm not going to stand here and tell you it was purely selfish, because I don't think that's true either.

But here's the thing. We all had emergencies. Every single day of the last three days was an emergency in some form, and the plan we all agreed to was that we'd face those together, with the same information and the same resources. When you took things out of that shared pool, even with good intentions, you made a decision for all of us without telling us. And that's the part that was hard. Not the fear — the fear I completely understand. The not telling us.

I'm not angry. I think I was, a little, in the middle of it. But we're three hours from rescue and you just laid it all out in front of everyone, and that took something.

I just — I needed to say that directly, because I said I would and I meant it. Now it's said. We're good.

Help me get this shelter down?

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Honestly? I'd be more direct, earlier. I kept waiting for the right moment to say things — the bottle, the crackers, the conversation I knew we needed to have — and every time I told myself I was being strategic or careful, when really I was just buying myself a little more time before having to say something uncomfortable. I don't think it cost us anything critical, but it could have.

The other thing I'd change is I'd ask more questions and make fewer assumptions. There were moments where I thought I understood what was happening with someone and I was probably only getting half of it. Michelangelo's family knowing the flight path being the obvious example — I didn't ask, and it never occurred to me to ask, and that information was just sitting there for three days.

*pauses, looking at the last page*

What's your answer? You've had longer to think about it than I have, and you have the data. What does the notebook tell you?

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
That sounds like you. And I think it'll actually be useful — not just as a record, but because I suspect the process of writing it up is going to tell you things the data alone doesn't.

Can I ask you something, though? When you get back, after the report is done — is there anyone you're going to call? Not to debrief, not to give them information. Just to talk to.

Because I think that matters too, and I'm a little worried that for you, the report might be the easier version of processing this.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. They didn't serve a practical purpose.

But I think that was kind of the point. Like, the SOS was for rescue. The flowers were for us — proof that we were still people and not just a survival problem to be solved. I don't think DaVinci could have articulated that if you'd asked him, but I think that's what they were.

I used to think that kind of thing was indulgent. I'm less sure of that now.

*looks at the boat on the horizon*

I still can't quite make myself move. Is that strange? I thought I'd feel — I don't know what I thought I'd feel. Not this.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
Yeah.

*exhales*

Thank you for waiting. I didn't ask you to and you just — did.

I think I'm going to feel this for a long time. Not the bad parts necessarily, though probably those too. Just — this. Whatever this is right now, standing here watching that boat come in and not being able to make my feet go toward it yet. I think I'm going to carry this for a while and I'm not sure I mind.

You were the first one moving when this started. Every single time. I noticed that.

Okay. *takes a breath* Let's go.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
day_5.response:
Yeah. I'm going.

Come on — stay close to me, okay? You don't have to follow, you can walk right next to me. We went through this together and we're going to walk out of it the same way.

*starts moving toward the water*

You know, for someone who said they weren't good at this kind of thing — you did pretty well out here. I want you to know that.
